tip: 'Estar' for temporary states. The square is full now, but it won't always be.
Subject after the verb! 'lo arregló mi padre' fronts the fix and saves the fixer for last – Spanish pushes the news to the end. English word order isn't law here.
'Para' here indicates destination: we left heading toward the airport.
'Nada es imposible' needs no extra 'no' – a negative word before the verb stands alone. After the verb, the double negative becomes mandatory: 'no hay nada'.
English blames "it" (it took me); Spanish makes YOU the subject: 'tardé' = I took-time. 'tardar en' + infinitive – the person doing it is the subject.
'Buscar' already contains the "for": 'busqué mi equipaje' = I looked FOR my luggage. The 'por' here means all over ('por toda la cinta') – never use 'por' to mean "for" after 'buscar'.
'Su' can mean his, her, their, or your ('usted'). Context decides – here 'su propio' pins it to each student. Spanish leaves this ambiguous where English can't.
'Hay' = there is/there are (invariable, same for singular and plural).
Languages go lowercase: 'español', never 'Español'. Spanish capitalizes much less than English – languages, nationalities, days, and months are all lowercase.
No "a" needed: 'soy vegetariano', not 'un vegetariano'. With 'ser' + identity (jobs, diets, religions), Spanish drops the article – you ARE the category itself.
Two verbs for spend: 'paso tres días' – 'pasar' for time, 'gastar' for money. Swap them and 'gasté tres días' suggests the days were burned through, wasted.
Clothes are plural in English, but 'ropa' is singular: 'hay ropa', 'la ropa está'. One shirt or a whole laundry load – still just 'ropa'.
Days carry their own article: 'los lunes' = Mondays. And no "on" – 'el lunes' is this Monday, 'los lunes' every Monday. Saying 'en lunes' is the English-speaker tell.
Why 'había', not 'hubo'? 'Había' paints the scene – the office sat empty all day. 'Hubo' would report a one-off event, which an ongoing state of emptiness isn't.
'¿Por dónde se va?' is literally "by where does one go?" – 'se' makes it impersonal, no "you" required. Spanish asks about the route, not the person walking it.
Breakfast is a verb: 'desayuné' = I breakfasted. No "have" needed – and it scales: 'almorzar' (lunch), 'cenar' (dinner). Each meal has its own verb.
How does 'lo dejó' (he left it) mean he quit? 'Dejar' = leave behind – Spanish quits things by walking away from them. 'fumaba mucho, pero lo dejó'.
'Con' fuses with just three pronouns: 'conmigo', 'contigo', 'consigo' – never 'con ti'. That -go tail is a Latin fossil: "with" got stuck on both ends of the word.
English drops one negative; Spanish stacks them. 'No existe nadie' is the required double – 'existe nadie' on its own would just sound broken, not emphatic.
'Quedamos' – 'quedar' normally means to remain, but between people it means we're meeting up. It's THE plan-making verb in Spain: 'quedamos a las ocho' seals the deal.
Not 'un astronauta'! Spanish drops the article for professions after 'ser': 'quería ser astronauta' – the a/an English demands just isn't there.
'Ahora bien' = now then / however. Introduces a reservation or counterpoint to what was just said.
'Saben de' = know about facts and fields: 'saben más de tecnología'. For knowing people or places, Spanish switches verbs to 'conocer' – knowledge vs acquaintance.
That tiny 'lo' in 'lo consigo' stands for the whole idea "not using my phone during meals". One pronoun can swallow an entire clause in Spanish.
'Embarazada' means pregnant – never embarrassed. It's the classic false friend: if you're embarrassed, say 'tengo vergüenza' or 'estoy avergonzada'.
'Es soltera' takes 'ser': marital status defines identity, not a passing state.
Wear or carry? Spanish doesn't care – 'llevar' does both. 'lleva gafas' = she wears glasses, literally "she carries glasses."
Why say "him" twice? 'pregúntale al recepcionista' = "ask-HIM to-the receptionist." Spanish doubles the person with 'le' even when they're named.
Windy isn't something it IS – it's something it MAKES. Weather often uses 'hacer': 'hace mucho viento' = it makes much wind.
No "a" before jobs! English says "I'm A designer"; Spanish drops the article with 'ser' + profession: 'soy diseñador gráfico.'
